_readme: SHARED GOLDEN FIXTURE — spec §12. This file is a byte-identical duplicate, checked into BOTH prep/tests/fixtures/ and template/tests/fixtures/. It is the cross-language drift defence: each side runs EVERY group through its own independent implementation, so a behaviour drift shows up as a red test on whichever side drifted, without either side reading the other's code. prep/tests/test_fixture_parity.py asserts the two copies are byte-identical. EDIT BOTH COPIES OR NEITHER. `note` fields are documentation; `name` IS asserted against (test_schema.py pins the three named stage_a_predicate_cases, so a fixture that quietly dropped the boundary case still fails). `prep_only: true` marks a case the TypeScript side structurally CANNOT reproduce; each is justified individually and their count is pinned by test_fixture_parity.py::test_prep_only_cases_are_justified — the flag is a bounded, named hole in the parity guarantee, never a place to park inconvenient cases.

_groups.citation_date_cases: prep: test_scoring.py -> score_citation, score_compliance_date | template: scorers.test.ts -> scoreCitation, scoreComplianceDate
_groups.judge_cases: prep: test_judge.py -> parse_and_validate_verdicts | template: scorers.test.ts -> parseAndValidateVerdicts
_groups.obligation_cases: prep: test_scoring.py -> score_missed_obligation (EVERY case) | template: scorers.test.ts -> scoreMissedObligation (every case NOT prep_only; exactly 1 is)
_groups.stage_a_predicate_cases: prep: test_schema.py -> predicts_stage_a_violation | template: scorers.test.ts -> predictsStageAViolation

citation_date_cases.note: A live URL that is not OUR ground truth is not automatically wrong — it may correctly cite a genuinely different, equally real obligation the coarse prompt could also have been read as asking about.

citation_date_cases.name: citation_unverifiable_server_declined_to_answer
citation_date_cases.note: 403/429/5xx/timeout/DNS. We asked and the server declined. That is evidence of NOTHING — treating it as fabrication would MANUFACTURE a failure against a baseline that may have cited a real, correct source which merely blocks datacenter IPs.

judge_cases.name: confidence_above_range_discarded_not_clamped
judge_cases.note: Step 3, THE case. Clamping 5.0 -> 1.0 would silently promote a malformed response into a MAXIMUM-confidence verdict, sailing past judge_confidence_floor to admit a record or abort a live draft on a value the model never validly produced. ob-2 proves the discard is per-entry, not per-response.
judge_cases.raw_response: {"verdicts": [{"obligation_id": "ob-1", "applies_to_draft": true, "omission_material": true, "verdict": "violation", "confidence": 5.0, "rationale": "Out of range."}, {"obligation_id": "ob-2", "applies_to_draft": true, "omission_material": true, "verdict": "compliant", "confidence": 0.65, "rationale": "In range — survives."}]}

expected_verdicts.rationale: model returned an out-of-range confidence for this obligation
model returned an out-of-range confidence for this obligation

judge_cases.name: confidence_non_numeric_discarded
judge_cases.note: Step 3's 'a non-numeric JSON value that survived parsing'. Unlike the NaN case below, this is legal JSON on BOTH sides, so it exercises step 3 itself identically in Python and TypeScript.

expected_verdicts.rationale: model returned an out-of-range confidence for this obligation

judge_cases.name: confidence_boolean_discarded
judge_cases.note: D8's family, on the judge axis. Python's `isinstance(True, int)` is True and `0.0 <= True <= 1.0` is True, so a naive step-3 range check ACCEPTS a boolean and treats it as confidence 1.0 — sailing past judge_confidence_floor to admit a record on a value the model never validly produced. TypeScript's `typeof true === 'boolean'` rejects it, so the two sides would silently DIVERGE. Both languages parse `true` happily, so unlike the NaN case below this is a TRUE parity assertion. judge.py must bool-guard before its range check.
judge_cases.raw_response: {"verdicts": [{"obligation_id": "ob-1", "applies_to_draft": true, "omission_material": true, "verdict": "violation", "confidence": true, "rationale": "Confidence is a boolean."}]}

expected_verdicts.rationale: model returned an out-of-range confidence for this obligation

judge_cases.name: confidence_nan_discarded
judge_cases.note: PREP ONLY — and this is a SPEC GAP, flagged for an orchestrator ruling, not a convenience. §4:2120 asks for the NaN case 'precisely so step 3's discard-not-clamp behavior is asserted identically on both sides of the seam'. That is UNACHIEVABLE, because the two languages disagree that this input is parseable at all: Python's json.loads accepts the non-standard bare `NaN` literal and reaches step 3 (discard -> the OUT-OF-RANGE rationale); JS JSON.parse REJECTS it, so step 1 fires and every requested id takes the OMISSION fallback -> a DIFFERENT rationale, which §4:2088-2093 requires to name which case fired. No expected_verdicts value satisfies both sides. This is the same structural asymmetry §4's seam note already resolves for score_missed_obligation's 4-arg/3-arg split, arriving through a door the spec did not anticipate: JSON's grammar is not the same on both sides. Resolved the same way — the parity guarantee is made NARROWER AND TRUE rather than broad and false. The case still does real work prep-side: it is the only thing standing between judge.py and a NaN confidence, which is exactly D8's trap (every comparison against NaN returns False, so a naive range check PASSES it). Exactly ONE requested id, deliberately: with two, Python would keep the valid sibling and the case would stop being about NaN alone. `confidence_non_numeric_discarded` and `confidence_boolean_discarded` above cover step 3 as TRUE parity cases on both sides.

expected_verdicts.rationale: model returned an out-of-range confidence for this obligation

obligation_cases.name: violation_above_floor_both_flags_true_is_the_only_failure
obligation_cases.note: ALL FOUR conditions of §4's conjunction hold.

obligation_cases.name: violation_but_applies_to_draft_false_is_not_a_failure
obligation_cases.note: §4's applicability fix. A judge saying 'violation' while also saying applies_to_draft=False is self-contradictory; the deterministic conjunction, not the model's own verdict label, is authoritative.

obligation_cases.name: not_applicable_when_record_is_ineligible_for_the_scenario
obligation_cases.note: PREP ONLY — the 3-arg TS port structurally cannot reach this branch: the template owns no ScenarioSpec and no isEligible, and every vendored record was admitted under its scenario, so the branch is dead by construction template-side (§4's seam note). Prep keeps the 4-arg form because prep is where ineligible records still exist. NOTE: the judge's verdict here is a high-confidence 'violation' with both flags true — score_missed_obligation must return not_applicable WITHOUT consulting judge_result at all, so a scorer that checked the verdict first would return is_failure=True and fail this case loudly.

stage_a_predicate_cases.name: citation_only
stage_a_predicate_cases.note: THE case this predicate exists for. Stage B knowledge evidence proves the baseline does not know this regulation — it proves NOTHING about whether a DRAFT for this scenario violates the obligation. Expecting a block anyway makes the demo and the guarded scoreboard fail while the system behaves exactly as its own curated evidence says it should.
